indexHeader: Firmware that makes your hardware shine.
indexFirst: We write firmware for devices that have to keep working, whether it’s your first prototype or a product that’s already out in the field. We’re based in the Eindhoven region.
indexSecond: Don’t have a board yet? We can design that too, so you work with one engineer from the first schematic to the updates in the field.
benefitFirst: Hardware and firmware under one roof
benefitSecond: Updates that can’t brick a device
benefitThird: Ready for the Cyber Resilience Act
problemsText: But when it freezes, misbehaves, or just won’t talk to other devices, people assume the whole thing is bad. We get it. Debugging firmware under pressure isn’t fun, and those little issues can make or break your product’s reputation.
problemsHighlight: We make sure the firmware does your hardware justice.
solutionHeader: We bring the same care to your firmware that you bring to your hardware.

homeCra.title: The CRA is already here.
homeCra.text: If you sell connected devices in the EU, exploited vulnerabilities now have to be reported within 24 hours. From December 2027 your products also need secure updates, an SBOM and a few other things. It sounds like a lot, but most of the work lands on the firmware, and that’s where we can help.
homeCra.read: What the CRA means for firmware

hardware.title: PCB Design & Board Bring-up
hardware.description: From the schematic to a board that boots, designed by the same people who write its firmware.
hardware.longDescription: We design boards in KiCad, usually around an ESP32 or RP2040 with USB-C and battery charging, and then bring them up: first power-on, clocks, peripherals and the first drivers. Since the same team does the hardware and the firmware, nobody has to guess which side a bug is on.
points: KiCad schematic and layout, 2 and 4 layers
Production files for JLCPCB: Gerbers, BOM and pick-and-place
Bring-up, first drivers and a written bring-up report

firmware.title: RTOS & Embedded Linux Firmware
firmware.description: Firmware and connectivity that stay up in the field.
firmware.longDescription: This is most of what we do. FreeRTOS on Cortex-M and ESP32, embedded Linux on Raspberry Pi and custom boards, and getting them to talk over Ethernet, Wi-Fi and MQTT. We write the drivers, track down the nasty bugs in memory, timing and networking, and leave you with code your team can actually maintain.
points: Drivers, RTOS tasks and protocol stacks
Ethernet, Wi-Fi and MQTT device-to-cloud links
Debugging crashes, memory leaks and timing issues
firmware.proof: We’re core developers on a production i.MX RT IoT gateway, which has shipped 199 releases since 2025.

updates.title: Secure Updates & CRA Readiness
updates.description: Field updates that can’t brick a device, ready for the Cyber Resilience Act.
updates.longDescription: Updating a device in the field shouldn’t feel like a gamble. Since September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act also requires you to report exploited vulnerabilities, and from December 2027 connected products need secure updates, an SBOM and a support period. We build the update path, with signed images, A/B slots and automatic rollback, and set up the SBOM and vulnerability handling around it.
points: CRA gap assessment with a prioritized roadmap
Signed A/B updates with automatic rollback
SBOM generated in CI and a vulnerability-handling runbook
updates.proof: We built the over-the-air bootloader and firmware updates for a production IoT gateway, and an A/B loader with automatic rollback for a fleet of Raspberry Pi kiosks.

modernization.title: Firmware Modernization
modernization.description: Get old firmware tested and easy to change again.
modernization.longDescription: Old toolchains, no tests, and only one person who really understands the code. Sound familiar? We go through the firmware, move it step by step to modern C++ (or Rust where it makes sense), and add tests that run on a PC and on real hardware in CI. After that, changes stop being scary.
points: Code audit with a prioritized report
Host-side unit tests and hardware-in-the-loop tests in CI
Incremental rewrites to modern C++ or Rust
modernization.proof: We built hardware-in-the-loop update tests for a production IoT gateway. They run in Jenkins on every change.

ai.title: AI for Engineering Teams
ai.description: Help your firmware team get real value out of AI coding tools, without skipping the testing on real hardware.
ai.longDescription: AI coding tools like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot can save an embedded team a lot of time, but only if they know your project and their changes still get tested on real hardware. We run hands-on workshops and set up your repository for it, with project knowledge files and review rules. We also give Software Engineering in Practice, a three-part training on foundations, resilience and production.
points: Workshop on AI-assisted embedded development
Repository setup: agent instructions, knowledge bases and guardrails
Software Engineering in Practice training with certificates
ai.proof: We set up the agent instructions and knowledge base for a production firmware project, and its developers use them every day.

fintech.title: FinTech & Payment Systems
fintech.description: Payment terminals, vending machines and kiosks that handle money reliably.
fintech.longDescription: When a payment device fails, someone loses money, and usually some trust too. We build firmware for payment terminals, vending machines and self-service kiosks, from the payment flow and stock tracking to secure communication and updates that don’t take a machine offline.

manufacturing.title: Industrial & Manufacturing
manufacturing.description: Connected machines that report what they’re doing and keep running.
manufacturing.longDescription: Factory machines run for years, and nobody wants a line to stop because of a firmware bug. We build controllers and gateways that collect machine data, send it over Ethernet or MQTT, and keep running through power cuts, network drops and updates.

defense.title: Defense & Aerospace
defense.description: Predictable software, with the testing and paperwork to back it up.
defense.longDescription: Defense and aerospace software has to behave the same way every time, and you need the tests and documentation to show it. We’ve worked on avionics programs, and we bring the same discipline to every project, whatever the industry.

automotive.title: Automotive & Mobility
automotive.description: Firmware and lab tooling for vehicle development.
automotive.longDescription: A lot of vehicle development happens on lab benches, flashing and netbooting boards all day, and that tooling just has to work. Automotive engineers use our open-source TFTP server and client, and we build firmware and lab tools with the same real-time and reliability needs in mind.

kiosk.title: Field updates that can’t brick a device
kiosk.challenge: A fleet of Raspberry Pi kiosks needed remote updates and provisioning, with nobody on site to recover a device when an update goes wrong.
kiosk.work: We built the loader that looks after the kiosk software. It keeps two app slots and rolls back on its own when a new version keeps failing. Around it there’s a 21-step provisioning script you can safely run again, a systemd watchdog, and a Jenkins and Docker pipeline that checks every release before it goes out.
kiosk.result: 18 releases in 18 months, all rolled out remotely. If one fails, the kiosk rolls itself back.

tftpd.title: A TFTP server automotive engineers build on
tftpd.challenge: Netbooting with U-Boot and flashing boards needs a small TFTP server and client you can rely on, running on any machine in the lab.
tftpd.work: We wrote rs-tftpd from scratch in pure Rust, with a matching client and support for the RFC 2347–2349 and 7440 options, and we maintain it as an open-source project.
tftpd.result: It’s packaged for NixOS and openSUSE, and engineers from Renault Software Labs, Ampere and Nokia have contributed to it. Renault uses the client as a library, and its duplicate-packets option cut an Apache NuttX network boot from 4 minutes to 20 seconds.

hardware.servicesTitle: Four ways to catch problems before your boards arrive.

review.label: Design review in 48 hours
review.lead: A second pair of eyes on your schematic and layout, with the datasheets open.
review.text: Send us your KiCad project, or the schematic and Gerbers. Within 48 hours you get a written review of the schematic and layout, plus an EMC pre-compliance check. For every finding we tell you exactly where it is, which datasheet line it comes from and how to fix it. We agree on a fixed price before we start.
points: Schematic checked against the datasheets: pin functions, ratings, strap pins, supply sequencing
Layout checked for power paths, return paths, decoupling, fab rules and assembly
EMC pre-compliance screening with located findings
A written report with coordinates and a fix for each finding
review.proof: Our Paper Calendar board already passed every design check, and the EMC check still found 6 warnings, each with its location and a fix.
callouts: A via where an SPI line changes layer, 7 mm from the nearest return-path capacitor

board.proof: Our Paper Calendar is a 4-layer ESP32-S3 board with a 50-pin e-paper connector, a charger, a fuel gauge and an audio amplifier. It’s been in manufacturing at JLCPCB since October 2026.

firmware.label: Firmware tested before the board exists
firmware.lead: Run your real firmware against your circuit, weeks before the boards arrive.

Test scripts press buttons, drain the battery, drop the network or skip ahead a few days, then check what the pins, buses, console and display did. Each CPU core is checked against QEMU, instruction by instruction.
points: ESP32-S3 and ESP32-C3, RP2040, i.MX RT1024 with Ethernet, AVR
Scenarios for power, buttons, network and display
Pixel-exact checks of what the display shows
Runs headless, so it becomes a check in your CI
firmware.proof: The Paper Calendar’s production firmware boots all the way through in the emulator. All 7 scenarios and 68 checks pass, down to the exact image on the e-paper.

emc.label: EMC, SI and PI pre-compliance
emc.lead: Find what the compliance lab would find, while a fix is still cheap.
emc.text: Rules of thumb only get you so far, so we wrote our own field solvers for circuit boards. They work out trace impedance and crosstalk from 2D cross-sections, the impedance of your power planes with the decoupling capacitors you actually placed, how return current flows around slots and gaps, and full 3D fields on the GPU for the critical spots. Every finding comes with its location and a fix. These are pre-compliance estimates that lower the risk of a lab visit, not a certification.
points: Trace impedance and crosstalk from the real stackup
Power-network impedance against a target, with the capacitors you placed
Return current and the loop inductance a slot adds
3D full-wave fields for the regions that matter
emc.proof: We checked the solvers against known answers. Single traces land within 0.3 % of the textbook formulas, stripline within 0.001 % of the exact solution and plane resonances within 0.06 % of the analytic cavity. On differential pairs with real copper, they showed that the usual closed-form formula reads 4 to 13 % low, which openEMS confirmed.
emc.slotCaption: A trace crossing a 20 mm slot in the ground plane (a made-up example). The return current has to go around the slot, which adds 2.3 nH and 0.15 V of noise for a 3.3 V, 1 ns edge.
emc.pdnCaption: The 3V3 rail seen from the ESP32-S3 with the board’s real decoupling: above the 0.66 ohm target from 136 MHz, peaking at 2.3 ohm.
emc.fdtdCaption: The electric field 0.8 mm above the board at 1 GHz, where the EPD_SCK line changes layer, from our own 3D full-wave solver (the inner planes simplified as solid).

hardware.mapText: This is the EMC check of the Paper Calendar on its real copper, with six numbered warnings and 23 information items, each at its exact spot. No vague notes about “the board”: every finding points at a place you can open in your layout tool.
hardware.caseLead: Our own e-paper calendar: ESP32-S3, 4 layers, in manufacturing at JLCPCB.
hardware.caseText: We built it with the same tools we use for customers, so we know what they catch and what they miss. The design passed all our checks without errors, and its firmware runs all the way through in the emulator against its own circuit. Then the EMC check found things a normal review wouldn’t even look for.

caseFacts.label: scenarios / assertions passing in the emulator
EMC warnings, each with coordinates and a fix

findings: Five vias where the e-paper SPI lines change layer are 6.2 to 9.5 mm from the nearest stitching capacitor (limit 3 mm at a 1 ns edge). Fix: a 100 nF capacitor within 3 mm of each, or one routing layer.
42 mm of the top edge has no ground via. Fix: two or three ground vias.
The 3V3 plane impedance first exceeds its 0.66 ohm target at 136 MHz at the ESP32-S3, where the module’s own decoupling takes over.
checked: No fast net crosses a gap in its reference plane
Every supply pin has its capacitor within 5 mm
The e-paper booster loops are about 2.6 nH and return in the plane
hardware.caseNote: The warnings assume a 1 ns edge, the fastest the check considers. Measuring the real edge on the first boards will settle them. That’s how we hand over every finding: what we know, what we assumed and how to find out for sure.

impedance.title: Free PCB Trace Impedance Calculator with a Real Field Solver
impedance.description: Calculate the impedance of PCB traces with a 2D field solver, not a formula: microstrip, stripline, differential pairs and coplanar waveguide. It runs in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere.
impedance.lead: Most online calculators evaluate a closed-form formula fitted to a handful of cases. This one solves the electromagnetic field of your exact cross-section, copper thickness and solder mask included, with the same field solver we use on our own boards.

kinds.stripline: Stripline (inner layer, planes above and below)

hints.gap: edge of the trace to the ground

impedance.drawingLabel: Cross-section of the trace with its dimensions
impedance.useSolved: Use this {what} in the impedance calculation
impedance.compareSame: The closed-form formula most calculators use gives {cf} Ω, within {pct} % of the field solver.
impedance.compareLower: The closed-form formula most calculators use gives {cf} Ω, which is {pct} % lower than the field solver, because a fitted formula only approximates your exact cross-section.
impedance.compareHigher: The closed-form formula most calculators use gives {cf} Ω, which is {pct} % higher than the field solver, because a fitted formula only approximates your exact cross-section.
impedance.compareWidthSame: The closed-form formula most calculators use would give a width of {cf}, almost the same.
impedance.compareWidthNarrower: The closed-form formula most calculators use would give a width of {cf}, which is {pct} % narrower than the field solver finds.
impedance.compareWidthWider: The closed-form formula most calculators use would give a width of {cf}, which is {pct} % wider than the field solver finds.
impedance.compareMask: The formula has no solder mask, so part of the difference is the mask.
impedance.compareStripline: The stripline formula assumes a strip of zero thickness, so part of the difference is the copper.

impedance.solved: Solved in {ms} ms in your browser, {n} panels.

impedance.badInput: Enter a positive number in every highlighted field.
impedance.unreachable: No value of that dimension reaches the target for this stack-up. Try a different target, or change another dimension.
impedance.solverError: The solver could not handle these dimensions.

how.title: A field solver, not a formula
how.text: Your cross-section is cut into small panels along the copper and the dielectric boundaries. The solver computes how charge spreads over them for each way of driving the traces, and impedance, effective permittivity and delay follow from the capacitance it finds.

how.title: Running in your browser
how.text: The solver is the one we use on our own boards, compiled to WebAssembly: a module of under 200 kB that your browser downloads once and runs locally. Nothing you type leaves the page, and there is no server to wait for.

how.title: Where the formula goes wrong
how.text: Closed-form formulas are curves fitted to a limited range, and they treat copper thickness roughly. For a 0.2 mm trace pair with a 0.15 mm gap on 0.2104 mm prepreg and 35 µm bare copper, the common formula gives 99.3 Ω differential and the solver 103.6 Ω. With a thinner dielectric the gap can reach 13 %.

impedance.limits: The result is for an ideal rectangular trace with a constant dielectric. Real boards have etched, trapezoidal traces, resin and glass that vary, and fab tolerances of around 10 %. Use your fab’s stack-up values, and let them confirm the final width.
impedance.ctaHeader: Want the whole board checked, not just one trace?
impedance.ctaText: The same solvers run through our hardware services: design review, controlled impedance, power integrity and EMC pre-compliance, before the board goes to the fab.
